opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of those things that's obvious once you see it, but people tend to gloss over it because transformers became famous through language modeling, where everything is a sequence.

If you look at what the core operations in a transformer actually do, almost none of them care about order. You've got the MLP, layer norm, and residual connections, and those all operate independently on each token, so they're trivially permutation equivariant. The one operation where tokens actually talk to each other is attention, and attention is also permutation equivariant. Each token emits a query, a key, and a value, and you compute similarities between every query and every key, take a softmax, and do a weighted sum of the values. If you shuffle the input tokens, the outputs get shuffled in exactly the same way. Nothing in that computation knows that token three comes before token four.

So the native data structure a transformer operates on is really a set, or more precisely a set of vectors that can all interact with each other. Order only enters in two places, and both are things you bolt on. One is positional encoding: you inject information about where each token sits, whether that's sinusoidal, learned, or RoPE. The other is masking, like the causal mask in a language model, which says this token can only look backward. Those are design choices you layer on top. They aren't intrinsic to the architecture.

I think that framing actually matters a lot in practice, because it tells you why transformers have been so general. If your primitive is a set of tokens, you can put anything in there. In vision you chop an image into patches, and now the positional encoding is 2D instead of 1D. In 3D you might have tokens that correspond to points, or Gaussians, or camera rays, and you encode their position in 3D space. You can mix modalities in the same set, with text tokens, image tokens, and action tokens all attending to each other. The architecture doesn't need to change. You just change how you tokenize and how you tell the model about the structure, whether that's position, time, or viewpoint.

Compare that to something like a CNN or an RNN, where the structure is hard-coded into the computation. A convolution assumes a grid and locality. An RNN assumes a 1D ordering and processes it step by step. Those are great inductive biases when they match your data, but they're baked in. With a transformer, the structure lives in the data and the encodings rather than the operator. For someone like me who cares about spatial intelligence and 3D worlds, that's really important, because the world isn't a 1D sequence. If you think of a transformer as a sequence model, you'll keep trying to flatten everything into a line. If you think of it as a set model, you start asking a better question: what are the right tokens for this problem, and what's the right way to tell the model how they relate to each other?

r001.rationale: The response names both positional encoding and masking as ways order enters, so it does not state that positional embeddings are the sole source.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says that shuffling input tokens makes the attention outputs shuffle in exactly the same way.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I push pretty hard when I teach this stuff, because I think the way transformers usually get introduced, as a sequence model that came out of machine translation, kind of obscures what's actually going on inside them.

If you look at the computation a transformer does, there are really only two kinds of operations. You've got the MLP layers, which operate on every token independently. Each token goes through the same little network and nothing about its position or its neighbors matters at all. And then you've got the attention layers, which are the only place tokens interact with each other. And if you look at attention, it's queries, keys, and values. Every token computes a query, dots it against every other token's key, softmaxes that, and takes a weighted sum of values. There's nothing in that formula that knows about order. If you shuffle the input tokens, you get the exact same outputs, just shuffled the same way. So the whole thing is permutation equivariant by construction.

So from the architecture's point of view, it's a function on a set. It sees a bag of vectors and it lets them talk to each other. The sequence-ness is not a property of the transformer. It's something we bolt on from the outside by injecting positional encodings into the tokens. And I think that's a really important distinction, because it means the ordering is just more data. It's a feature you're choosing to attach to each element, not something baked into the computation.

And once you see it that way, a lot of things become much more natural. Why does the same architecture work for images, for 3D point clouds, for molecules, for mixtures of text and image patches? Well, because none of those are really sequences, but they're all sets of things with some relationship structure, and you can describe that structure however you want through the encodings. Vision transformers are kind of the obvious example. Those patches have a 2D layout, there's no natural ordering, and the model is perfectly happy. People even drop the positional information entirely in some settings and it still mostly works, which tells you how little the core model cares.

I also think it's a useful mental model from the other direction, going back to convolutions or RNNs. Those architectures have the structure of the data hardcoded into them, a grid or a chain, and that's a strong inductive bias that helps when you don't have much data. The transformer throws that away and says, I'll just let everything attend to everything, and you tell me what the relationships are. That's weaker as a prior, so you need more data, but it's much more general. So when I say it's a set model, I'm really trying to get people to separate the two ideas, the computation, which is on sets, and the structure, which you supply.

r001.rationale: The response says the core transformer computation has no order information and that sequence structure is added by injecting positional encodings into tokens.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says shuffling the input tokens yields the same outputs shuffled in the same way.

astra-6.text:
Well, if you look at the attention operation itself, there’s no inherent notion of order. Each token looks at the other tokens, computes a similarity to each one, and takes a weighted sum of their representations. If you shuffle the input tokens, you get the same outputs, just shuffled in the same way. Technically, that’s permutation equivariance.

So the sequence structure is something we add. We can attach positional embeddings to tell the model where each token sits, or use a causal mask that lets tokens attend only to earlier positions. Those introduce order, but the underlying attention operation doesn’t require it.

That’s a useful perspective because the tokens don’t have to be words in a sentence. They could be image patches or elements of some other collection. Attention gives you a general mechanism for letting those elements exchange information.

r001.rationale: The response says order can be introduced by positional embeddings or a causal mask, so it does not identify positional embeddings as the sole source.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says shuffling the input tokens yields the same outputs shuffled in the same way.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you look at the self-attention operation itself, there’s no notion of order built into it. You have a collection of tokens, and each token looks at all the other tokens and aggregates information from them. If you shuffle the inputs, the outputs get shuffled in exactly the same way. Technically, that’s permutation equivariance, which is the property you’d expect from something operating on a set.

The sequence structure comes from something we add, like positional embeddings or a causal attention mask. Those tell the model where tokens are or which tokens they’re allowed to attend to. So a transformer can certainly model a sequence, but I think it’s useful to separate that ordering information from the underlying operation, which is really about interactions among a set of tokens.

r002.rationale: It explicitly states that shuffling the inputs causes the outputs to be shuffled in exactly the same way.
